title: Teaching on Purpose No Rounding Up
author: Kohlbeck, Adam
summary: At Chiltern Learning Trust, we have six core purposes that capture everything teachers do: Securing, maintaining and regaining attention Communicating meaning Driving hard thinking Enable and scaffold practice Utilising memory Checking for understanding Each week, I interview one of our teachers on the 'Teaching on purpose' podcast about a technique they commonly use to serve one of our six core purposes and I write about it here... Thanks for reading Adam's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. This week's purpose: Driving hard thinking This week's technique: No Rounding up This week, I spoke to Lynsey Steadman about her thoughts on the importance of driving students to think hard and she didn't disappoint. Thinking takes time to develop... Thinking about something new or a new connection between two different but familiar concepts requires time. The first thought we have when we are making new connections is rarely the best or final thought that we have. There is a process of trying out an initial thought or idea, iterating it through correction and adjustment in real time before settling on an improved version of it. Children need the time to engage in this whole, (often not very aesthetically pleasing) process and as teachers, we need to ensure we provide this space. When teachers ask students a question that requires an element of synthesis, for example: How is ambition shown in both a positive and negative sense in Macbeth? We are asking them to pull together two banks of knowledge that we know are connected but students may not be as clear on what precisely the connection is. We need to provide the space to do that messy cognitive work of sense-making and connection drawing. Often, students will initially provide a partial answer, for example: ''It's positive because it is what Macbeth uses to become powerful and negative...'' Upon seeing that pause, teachers can feel the pressure to round up the answer - finishing it off. For example: ''it's negative because that power ends up corrupting Macbeth''. There are a number of very well-intentioned reasons that a teacher might do this. They could be concerned for the student and not want them to feel put on the spot when they don't know the rest of the answer. Rounding up could be done to spare the student some potential embarrassment. The teacher may also be conscious of time and the need to move the lesson on, protecting the flow of the narrative of the lesson. Both of these reasons are plausible but they don't support learning and in fact, if rounding up becomes a routine feature of a teacher's practice, we risk sending the message that there is no need to think hard because your answer will always be rounded up in any case. So, what could we do instead? Lyndsey suggests that we use the technique, 'No rounding up' and avoid filling in the thinking gap for students. As ever, there is nuance in this technique but first, let's get clear on precisely what it is... No rounding up It's a simple technique really because it is mainly focused on not doing something rather than doing something. Instead of filling in the pause with the rest of the answer, the teacher remains patient, avoids the temptation to fill the space and allows the thoughts to ferment in the students' mind, completing their answer only when they are ready to. Of course, 'simple' doesn't mean 'easy' and the temptation to round up will be strong at times. It takes deliberate effort to step back and allow the thinking, even when it appears uncomfortable. Allowing students to sit in that thinking sends the message that you know the understanding is there and you are prepared to be patient to hear it. That is, despite the potential discomfort, a far more powerful message than the one they get when teachers round up their answer, seemingly anticipating an endless silence and an inability to access the answer. When might you use this technique as described? One example of when a teacher might use the 'No rounding up' technique is when asking about a process or system. This is the ideal kind of question because it requires the combination of component pieces of knowledge, brought together to arrive at the whole. For example: How does a metal conduct electricity? This question requires students to draw together component knowledge to fully explain the process of how metal conducts electricity and so there is some synthesis and connection to be done. Allowing them the space to do this thinking is crucial to their success in establishing a full and developed answer. The teacher avoids finishing off the student's initial attempt at a response, instead leaving the space free for the student to refine their initial thoughts. When might you adapt the technique? Of course, you can't always just back off and wait for a more developed answer. There are times where you pick up the sense that students' understanding is not as well developed around one or more of the components they need to draw together in their answer to the question you have asked. Where this is the case, teachers might choose to put in a short period of discussion with a partner, giving students time to rehearse their ideas verbally. Other times, even providing this talk time is not enough to help students arrive at the full understanding. It may be useful in these situations to make use of a word bank or sentence stems. These reduce the cognitive resources that students are expending in trying to formulate their answer, leaving more resources free for the thinking around the concept at the heart of the question they have been asked. These adaptations come down to knowing your students but also, knowing your curriculum. If you know that a concept you want them to know about is a threshold concept (not knowing it significantly limits the extent and coherence of future knowledge that can be gained in that topic) then over time, you must move students to a point where they are doing the full thinking themselves with minimal scaffolding. When might you not use this technique? 'No rounding up' is not the answer to all our challenges when trying to drive hard thinking. There are times when you know that students simply do not have the fluidity of core knowledge available in order to answer the question. When this is the case, driving hard thinking by providing the space and time to think deeply is unlikely to be effective in service of student learning because students have under-developed schema with which to do that thinking. In these cases, one technique that teachers could use is an 'everybody writes' where students use notes from previous lessons to draw together their ideas about how two or more component pieces of knowledge connect in answer to a question. This use of previous notes means that there is no retrieval practice gain available to students but if that knowledge was out of reach, there would have been no retrieval practice gain from allowing them the extended thinking time. When students do not have the knowledge required to do that synthesised piece of thinking, provide the time and space to instead, make those required connections deliberately in writing. So, if want to drive student thinking, 'No rounding up' might be one really powerful technique that we could use to do that. But, as ever, we need to be driven by our purpose and mediated by context to make sure that we choose the right technique, at the right time for the right reason.
